title: Haemoconcentration ("red biliary")
definition: Haemoconcentration ("red biliary") is a haematocrit that is high, or within the reference interval but too high for the degree of haemolysis, in a dog with intravascular haemolysis (haemoglobinuria or haemoglobinaemia) [R1][R2]. It is a rare complication, described almost only in B. rossi infection, with a high mortality [R3][R4].
definition_note: Working definition confirmed in substance, with three changes. No single threshold exists: 0.37, 0.47 and 0.55 L/L are all in use [R2][R1][R3]. A 'normal' haematocrit that is inappropriate for the haemolysis is included [R1]. The sources link it mainly to acute kidney injury and cerebral signs; a direct link with lung oedema was not documented in any study [R1][R5].
key_points: Suspect it in any dog with haemoglobinuria whose haematocrit is high or normal; a haematocrit above 0.55 L/L gave an odds ratio for death of 32.7 in 320 B. rossi dogs [R3].
It is rare: 4 of 320 dogs (1.3%) in the largest B. rossi cohort and 3 of 35 in another [R3][R2].
It is thought to be plasma loss through leaky endothelium, not simple dehydration, and it comes with organ failure, mainly kidney and brain [R3][R1][R5].
No treatment was ever tested in haemoconcentrated dogs; all fluid advice on this page is level D or E [R6][R7].
In human severe malaria, liberal fluid loading did not correct acidosis or kidney function and was followed by lung oedema; give fluids in small boluses and reassess after each [R8][R9][R7].
Reported mortality is above 30% in referral data and usually above 80% in a practitioner survey [R4][R10].

description.heading: What it is
description.text: A dog with obvious intravascular haemolysis whose haematocrit is above the reference interval, or normal when it should be low [R1][R2]. South African practitioners call it 'red' biliary [R10]. Reviews class it as a complication of complicated babesiosis, beside acute kidney injury, cerebral babesiosis and ARDS [R1][R5][R11].

description.heading: How common, and in which dogs
description.text: In a 1993 survey, 94 of 155 South African practices (60.6%) had seen 'red' biliary [R10]. In a hospital series of 662 B. rossi cases, 18% of hospitalised dogs were not anaemic and were often polycythaemic [R12]. In recent Onderstepoort cohorts it was 4 of 320 dogs (1.3%) and 3 of 35 dogs [R3][R2]. It was present in 2 of 20 dogs with babesial pancreatitis [R13]. Practitioners linked it to Staffordshire bull terriers, an unverified observation [R10].

description.heading: When in the course of disease
description.text: In the cohorts it was found at admission, in samples taken before any treatment [R3][R2]. An experimental B. rossi infection model used it as a criterion to stop the experiment and treat [R14].

description.heading: Mechanism
description.text: The cause is not known. The 320-dog cohort found that it was not explained by significant dehydration, that it always came with multiple organ failure, and proposed plasma loss through an excessively permeable endothelium [R3]. Reviews describe vasculitis and a shift of fluid from the vessels to the tissues [R1][R5]. Non-anaemic dogs had severe azotaemia, electrolyte changes and a weak leucocyte response, which the authors read as an overwhelming inflammatory response rather than haemolytic disease [R12].

species_notes.note: All primary data on this page are from B. rossi in South Africa [R3][R2][R12][R15]. A review that compares the Babesia species of dogs describes it as a rare form of B. rossi disease with a very poor prognosis [R16]. South African papers before about 2006 name the parasite B. canis; B. rossi is inferred from the place.
A European review lists haemoconcentration among complications and attributes such complications mainly to B. rossi [R17]. No B. canis case series with haemoconcentration was found.
No report of the syndrome was found.

criteria.note: Highest Hct category in 320 B. rossi dogs (3 of 4 died); same cut-off used in an experimental B. rossi model as an end point.
Threshold given in a review of complicated babesiosis; no study behind the number was cited.

criteria.criterion: Haematocrit with macroscopic haemoglobinuria or haemoglobinaemia
criteria.note: Definition used in a prospective study of 35 B. rossi dogs; 3 met it at admission.

criteria.threshold: within the reference interval despite obvious haemolysis
criteria.note: Described in a review as carrying a very high mortality; no number is given, so this is a clinical judgement.

clinical_signs.note: Macroscopic haemoglobinuria or haemoglobinaemia is part of the definition.

clinical_signs.sign: Neurological signs, oliguria or anuria, dyspnoea
clinical_signs.note: Signs of the organ failures that accompany it: cerebral babesiosis, acute kidney injury, lung injury.
Collapse at admission gave an odds ratio for death of 8.36 in B. rossi; not reported separately for haemoconcentrated dogs.

tests.finding: High, or normal in a dog with haemoglobinuria.
tests.note: Take it before fluids or transfusion. In 19 treated uncomplicated cases the Hct fell in every dog, by a mean maximum of 0.046 L/L, most often at 6 or 12 h.

tests.test: Serum creatinine and urine specific gravity
tests.finding: Creatinine above 150 µmol/L without clinical dehydration marked renal involvement in one series; USG of 1.030 or more was read as prerenal azotaemia in another.
tests.note: Serum urea is raised in many B. rossi dogs for non-renal reasons; do not use it to diagnose kidney failure.

tests.finding: Cerebral babesiosis was defined as acute cerebral signs with normal or high glucose.
tests.note: Rules out hypoglycaemia as the cause of neurological signs.

tests.test: Arterial blood gas or pulse oximetry, thoracic radiographs
tests.finding: PaO2 below 60 mmHg, or A-a gradient above 15 mmHg on room air, or radiographic oedema, marked lung involvement.

differentials.condition: Dehydration from vomiting, diarrhoea or poor intake
differentials.distinguish: History of fluid loss. In B. rossi the haemoconcentration was not explained by significant dehydration. Concentrated urine (USG 1.030 or more) fits a prerenal cause.

differentials.condition: Early or uncomplicated babesiosis before the anaemia shows
differentials.distinguish: No organ failure; the haematocrit falls after treatment. A normal haematocrit with marked haemoglobinuria is not reassuring.

differentials.condition: Acute pancreatitis with gut fluid loss (SY12)
differentials.distinguish: Vomiting, abdominal pain; it can occur together with haemoconcentration.

differentials.condition: Cerebral babesiosis, acute kidney injury, ARDS
differentials.distinguish: These are companions of haemoconcentration, not alternatives: look for them in every haemoconcentrated dog.

approach.action: Measure PCV and look at urine and plasma
approach.detail: Do it on arrival, before fluids. A high PCV, or a normal PCV with haemoglobinuria, means haemoconcentration [R1][R2].
Check mentation, glucose, creatinine, urine output, USG, respiratory rate and SpO2. Haemoconcentration came with organ failure in every case of the large cohort [R3][R18].
Standard antibabesial treatment, as in TX00. The cohort dogs received diminazene aceturate [R3].

approach.action: Give fluids in small boluses and reassess
approach.detail: Isotonic crystalloid, starting with about one quarter of a shock volume, then reassess heart rate, CRT and blood pressure after each bolus [R7]. Avoid liberal loading: in human malaria it was followed by lung oedema [R8].

approach.action: Watch for fluid overload and falling urine output
approach.detail: Respiratory rate and effort, lung sounds, body weight, urine output and PCV. If a central line is in place, a CVP above 10 cmH2O suggests volume overload [R7].
Reviews describe these dogs as needing early, aggressive and intensive therapy; some need assisted ventilation [R11][R5].

treatments.name: Isotonic crystalloid in small titrated boluses
treatments.aim: Restore perfusion without adding to fluid leak into lungs and brain.
treatments.evidence_summary: No study tested fluids in haemoconcentrated dogs. A review recommends crystalloid and colloid support for complicated babesiosis [R5]. An older review discusses the problems of fluids in dogs with oliguria, cerebral signs or lung oedema [R6]. In a 1993 survey, 44% of South African practices used Ringer's lactate in complicated cases [R10]. The dose below is a general emergency textbook rule, not tested in babesiosis [R7].

doses.dose: one quarter of the shock volume (shock volume 90 mL/kg)
doses.frequency: initial volume, then titrate to response
doses.context: Dogs in hypovolaemic or haemorrhagic shock; emergency textbook, not babesiosis
doses.note: Reassess heart rate, CRT and blood pressure after each bolus. No source gives a rate for haemoconcentrated dogs.

treatments.cautions: Fluid loading can worsen lung oedema when vessels leak [R8][R9]. In complicated babesiosis with acute kidney injury or ARDS, volume expansion may be harmful [R5].
treatments.monitoring: Heart rate, CRT, blood pressure, urine output and PCV after each bolus. CVP should not rise by more than 5 cmH2O in 24 h [R7].

treatments.name: Hypertonic saline
treatments.aim: Expand plasma volume with a small volume of fluid.
treatments.evidence_summary: A 1995 review of supportive treatment considered hypertonic fluids for complicated babesiosis; only the abstract was read and it gives no dose [R6]. No study in dogs with babesiosis. The dose below is from an emergency textbook for head trauma and haemorrhagic shock [R7].

doses.context: Dogs with head trauma or haemorrhagic shock; emergency textbook, not babesiosis
doses.note: The textbook says to give it with another crystalloid or colloid, because its effect is short. The source is not consistent: one passage prints 0.7% at 4 mL/kg (taken as a misprint for 7%), and another gives 7.5% at 3 to 5 mL/kg IV over 10 to 15 minutes. Check the concentration on the product before use.

treatments.cautions: The textbook advises against it in interstitial dehydration [R7]. No safety data in babesiosis.
treatments.monitoring: Heart rate, CRT and blood pressure after the bolus [R7].

treatments.name: Liberal (large-volume) fluid loading
treatments.evidence_summary: Not studied in dogs. In 28 adults with severe falciparum malaria, liberal saline did not improve acidosis or kidney function; lung water rose in 17 of 22, and 8 developed lung oedema, of whom 5 died [R8]. In a trial of 3141 febrile African children (57% with malaria), fluid boluses raised 48-hour mortality (relative risk 1.45 against no bolus) [R9]. Human malaria evidence only.
treatments.cautions: Lung oedema can develop while the patient is still hypovolaemic or euvolaemic [R8].

treatments.name: Synthetic colloid (hydroxyethyl starch)
treatments.aim: Hold fluid in the vessels when plasma leaks.
treatments.evidence_summary: A review recommends colloid support in complicated babesiosis, with no data [R5]. In 180 ICU dogs given 10% HES 250/0.5 compared with 242 ICU dogs, HES was an independent risk factor for death or acute kidney injury (adjusted odds ratio 1.98, number needed to harm 6) [R20]. Not studied in babesiosis.

doses.frequency: bolus over 10 to 15 min, then reassess
doses.context: Dogs in shock; emergency textbook, not babesiosis
doses.note: Shown for completeness. A later dog cohort linked HES to death and kidney injury.

treatments.cautions: Risk of acute kidney injury and death in dogs [R20]; acute kidney injury already complicates many haemoconcentrated dogs [R1].

prognosis.text: Poor. In 320 B. rossi dogs, 3 of 4 with a haematocrit above 0.55 L/L died (deaths include euthanasia), against 14.2% of severely anaemic dogs [R3]. Referral data put mortality above 30% [R4]; practitioners reported it usually above 80% [R10]. Of 3 haemoconcentrated dogs in another study, 2 recovered and 1 with acute renal failure died [R15]. Death comes mainly from the organ failures that come with it [R18][R5].

indicators.meaning: Odds ratio for death 32.7 (95% CI 3.12 to 344), from only 4 dogs.
Odds ratio for death 62.4; all 6 cerebral cases in the 320-dog cohort died.

indicators.finding: Creatinine above 106 µmol/L, urea above 20 mmol/L
indicators.meaning: Odds ratios for death 7.55 and 30.95 in B. rossi.

indicators.finding: Renal or CNS involvement in complicated cases
indicators.meaning: Renal involvement gave a 5-fold and CNS involvement a 57-fold higher risk of death than other complications.

related.why: Acute kidney injury, which often comes with haemoconcentration.
Cerebral babesiosis, which often comes with haemoconcentration.
Lung oedema and ARDS, the main risk of fluid overload.
Shock and hypotension, and fluid resuscitation in general.
Complicated disease, triage and the order of care.
Acute pancreatitis, a differential and a companion complication.

evidence_gaps: No treatment of any kind was tested in haemoconcentrated dogs; the fluid advice is extrapolated.
No source gives a fluid rate, an end point or a fluid type for haemoconcentrated dogs.
No evidence was found for or against plasma transfusion in this syndrome.
No source addresses red cell transfusion in a haemoconcentrated dog that later becomes anaemic.
The haematocrit threshold differs between sources (0.37, 0.47, 0.55 L/L) and none was validated against outcome except in 4 dogs.
No study measured total protein, albumin or plasma volume in haemoconcentrated dogs, so plasma leak versus dehydration is not proven.
No primary report of the syndrome was found for B. canis, B. gibsoni or B. vogeli.
The link with lung oedema rests on review statements, not on data.

search.note: PubMed and Europe PMC searches for haemoconcentration or red biliary with babesiosis returned 4 and about 20 relevant records; all South African primary data were read. No treatment study of the syndrome exists, so fluid advice comes from a veterinary emergency textbook and human malaria trials. The 2024 AAHA fluid guideline and the full text of Jacobson 2006 could not be reached.
